chapter_theme: Twenty verses of three things each range from the minister's daily practice to the wife's debts, the passions that consume their holder, what counts as wealth and purity, and gifts wasted on those who lack their inner condition; again and again a good is measured by the giving, restraint or trust within the person rather than by outward rank.

61.reading: Conducting oneself so that the fivefold knowledge comes within reach, guarding in advance so that what threatens to arrive does not arrive, and knowing day by day the state of the kings who stand opposed are named the settled practice of great ministers of renown.
61.nuance: ஐயறிவும் is the hard word: it may be the knowledge of the five senses held in order, or fivefold learning a minister must have; either way the first item is a discipline of the self and the other two face outward, to the coming danger and the hostile king. The count word is the personal இம்மூவர் though the three things are practices, not persons.

items.claim: conducting oneself so that the fivefold knowledge is within one's grasp is a great minister's practice
guarding beforehand so that the threatened harm never arrives is a great minister's practice
knowing daily how the opposing kings stand is a great minister's practice

62.reading: The shameless man who does not weigh the worth of a kindness done him, the man who speaks crookedly in the public assembly before the worthy, and the man who wrongly keeps a deposit placed with him are named three who live on with their line of descendants lost.
62.nuance: எச்சம் இழந்து names the punishment in the next generation, not in the offender's own life: all three faults are breaches of trust (a kindness, a public judgment, a deposit), and the verse makes the loss of heirs their common wage.

items.claim: the shameless man who does not weigh a kindness's worth lives with his line cut off
the man who speaks crookedly in the assembly before the worthy lives with his line cut off
the man who wrongfully takes a deposit entrusted to him lives with his line cut off

63.reading: Friendship with those who do not shrink from causing pain, keeping in the house a bangled wife who dreads guests, and living beside people whose nature yields no worth are named three things that bring no good.
63.nuance: All three are about who lives near one: a friend, a wife, a neighbour. The wife's fault is not unchastity but fear of guests, so the house fails at the outward duty the next verse assigns her.

items.claim: friendship with those unafraid to hurt brings no good
keeping at home a bangled wife who shrinks from guests brings no good
living next to people of no worthy nature brings no good

64.reading: By tending good guests she is a friend, by daily caring for the household she is the mother who bore it, and by bearing children of an old family she is the mistress of the house: these three are named the debts a chaste wife has taken on.
64.nuance: Each duty earns a role (friend, mother, mistress), so the wife is three persons to the house; the closing word கடன் makes them owed, and கற்புடையாள் makes chastity the frame within which all three are counted.

items.claim: by tending good guests the chaste wife acts as a friend, and this is her debt
by caring for the household daily she acts as the mother who bore it, and this is her debt
by bearing children of an old family she is mistress of the house, and this is her debt

norm.note: a rule of the period for a wife's duties: hospitality, care of the house and bearing children are her debts as a chaste woman

65.reading: Fear rising like the wave-tossed sea, craving that cannot let go of what it has longed for, and anger that cannot see the true state of what is bound up with it are said to be the way one fries in one's own ghee.
65.nuance: The image is self-consumption: the fat that cooks one is one's own, so the three passions need no outside enemy. Fear stands where a quick reader expects confusion beside desire and anger.

items.claim: fear surging like the restless sea makes one fry in one's own ghee
craving that will not release what it has fastened on makes one fry in one's own ghee
anger blind to the true state of things makes one fry in one's own ghee

66.reading: The adornment of a woman who has no husband, the ring on the hand of a man who has no servant to walk behind him, and a king who lives having bent the sceptre he holds are named three things not joined with fitness.
66.nuance: கறை is uncertain: read as dark adornment, the first two items are both ornaments worn without the support that makes them fitting (a husband, a servant), and the king's bent sceptre becomes the same kind of empty sign; read as 'stain', the first item would be a widow's blame, and the parallel weakens.

items.claim: the adornment of a husbandless woman is not fitting
a ring on the hand of a man with no attendant is not fitting
a king who lives with his sceptre bent is not fitting

norm.note: a rule of the period on a woman without a husband: her adornment is counted unfitting

67.reading: A wife who stands against her husband, servants without proper nature, and kin who stand in fault are said to devour a man, as his hair greys, like the fruit of his old deeds, and there is nothing the sufferer can do about them.
67.nuance: முந்தை பழவினையாய் makes the three household troubles the shape that past karma takes, which is why the verse ends that the sufferer has no remedy: they are borne, not fixed.

items.claim: a wife who stands against her husband devours him like old karma
servants of no proper nature devour him like old karma
kin who persist in wrong devour him like old karma

68.reading: Having wealth that gives something to those who have nothing, the right way of one who considers the impermanence of this world, and the purity that does nothing painful to any creature are named three things found in people who know the good.
68.nuance: தூய்மை is defined here by an act toward others, not by bathing or diet: purity is harming no living thing.

items.claim: possessions that give to those who lack are found in those who know the good
a right path shaped by reflecting on impermanence is found in those who know the good
the purity of doing no hurt to any creature is found in those who know the good

69.reading: An ox that does hard work, a maiden of well-formed full body long kept at home, and a guest who arrives in distress having strayed from the road are named three things hard to come by.
69.nuance: The guest is counted as a prize, beside a draught ox and a marriageable girl, not as a burden; the lost and suffering guest is the most valued because he most needs the house.

items.claim: an ox that does arduous work is hard to obtain
a maiden of full, well-formed body long kept at home is hard to obtain
a guest who comes weary after losing the road is hard to obtain

norm.note: a period valuation of a young woman's body and seclusion, counted among prized possessions with the ox

70.reading: One who dug a tank for charity with a grove beside it, the brahmin who has reached the far shore of the Veda by recitation, and one who, avoiding evil, eats after sharing what he can are the three called rich.
70.nuance: Wealth is redefined as what one has given or mastered: a public work, learning held on the tongue, and food shared. பார்ப்பான் names a birth group, but the verse praises his learning and states no rule of rank.

items.claim: the man who dug a charitable tank with a grove is called rich
the brahmin who has mastered the Veda by recitation is called rich
the man who eats after sharing what he can, shunning wrong, is called rich

71.reading: The bathing of those who have no cloth to change into, women who take up and enter the disputation of the assembly, and the poverty of men who have the manliness to give and protect are named three things the poet's eye cannot bear to see.
71.nuance: The first person என் கண் is rare in the book. The line division is doubtful: பெண்டிர் may close the first item (women bathing without a change of cloth) rather than open the second; on the reading taken here, women in the assembly's contest are counted as an unbearable sight. காண அரிய could also mean simply 'rarely seen'.

items.claim: bathing by those who have no garment to change into is painful to see
women joining the contest of the assembly is painful to see
poverty in men whose manliness gives and protects is painful to see

norm.note: a period judgment that women entering the assembly's disputation is an unfitting sight

72.reading: Poverty fears the man of steady heart, ill-gotten wealth fears the man who keeps dharma in mind, and every creature fears the warrior: these three are named matters settled by strength.
72.nuance: The grammar is reversed from the expected: the man does not avoid poverty or wrong wealth, they avoid him, so his inner strength acts on things outside him the way the warrior's acts on creatures.

items.claim: poverty shrinks from the man of steady heart
wrongful wealth shrinks from the man who thinks of dharma
every creature fears the warrior

73.reading: The man who says he will make bright wealth by begging, the man who calls a woman who goes about with many his bond of love, and the man who sails across the wide sea are named three who live daring what is hard.
73.nuance: The sea voyage is a real risk set beside two risks of judgment, so begging for wealth and trusting a wanton woman are made as perilous as open water.

items.claim: the man who means to build wealth by begging dares the hard
the man who calls a woman of roving conduct his love-bond dares the hard
the man who goes through the wide sea dares the hard

norm.note: a period judgment on a woman's conduct: a woman who goes about widely is no fit bond

74.reading: The man who lives by killing and eating, the fool who presumes to embrace the great when they embrace, and the man who laughs at one who says 'I have nothing, give me something' are named three who hold fast to nothing.
74.nuance: கடைப்பிடியாதார் is the common fault: none keeps a rule. The second item is unsure: it may be the fool who takes the familiarity of the great as licence to be familiar himself, or one who clings only when the great cling to him.

items.claim: the man who lives by killing and eating keeps no rule
the fool who presumes on the great when they embrace him keeps no rule
the man who mocks one who asks for a gift keeps no rule

75.reading: Wealth in the hands of one bound to generosity, the books learned by one with understanding in his heart, and a leader who knows what is fitting in his alliances are named three trees whose wood has hardened without a hollow.
75.nuance: காழ்த்த மரம் is heartwood, prized for being solid through: the image values soundness within, not fruit given out. புணர்வு may be alliance, counsel or marriage, and the leader is left open.

items.claim: wealth held by one committed to generosity is solid heartwood
the learning of one with inner understanding is solid heartwood
the leader who knows what is fit in union is solid heartwood

76.reading: A guest who comes on a rainy day, a courtesan whose heart is elsewhere yet who never falls short in her business, and a servant who in his valour answers back against a command are named three who are hard to tend even when one tries.
76.nuance: Our text reads வருந்தும், which would make the first item 'the one who suffers on a rainy day'; the count and the sense want விருந்தும், the guest. The three are hard to keep for different reasons: the guest's need, the courtesan's divided heart, the servant's pride.

items.claim: a guest arriving on a rainy day is hard to tend
a courtesan whose heart is elsewhere yet keeps her trade is hard to keep
a servant who defiantly contradicts orders in his valour is hard to keep

norm.note: a period view of the courtesan as a woman whose divided heart makes her hard to keep

77.reading: Living out of reach of the base, keeping friendship with the good without forsaking them even in the dead of night, and carefully guarding that nothing scarring comes are named three things found only in those whose family is spotless.
77.nuance: The closing ஏ (உள்ளார்க்கே) restricts the three to the spotless family: the verse reads conduct as the sign of lineage rather than lineage as a licence.

items.claim: living beyond reach of the base is found only in a spotless family
holding to friendship with the good even at midnight is found only in a spotless family
guarding so that no scar of blame comes is found only in a spotless family

78.reading: Having purity is boldness, having truthfulness that drives off evil deeds is beauty, and not uttering evil in mind or speech: these three are named the practice of those who have grown strong in penance.
78.nuance: The first two items carry their own predicates (purity is boldness, truth is beauty) inside the count; துணிவாம் தொழிலகற்றும் could also be read together as 'truth that removes rash deeds', which would shift the first item's predicate.

items.claim: possessing purity, which is boldness, is the ascetic's practice
possessing truthfulness that drives off evil deeds, which is beauty, is the ascetic's practice
not voicing evil in mind or in speech is the ascetic's practice

79.reading: The man who lives without fearing blame, who is a cow; the man who through decline gave up the hard penance he took on; and the man who, having married, lives in fear of his wife, who is an ox: that these three eat rice is a sickness to the heart.
79.nuance: இவர்மூவர் is a personal form, so the cow and the ox are men called beasts; the predicate is that their being fed at all grieves the onlooker. The first item could instead be the cow of a blameless-fearless man, which the count word argues against.

items.claim: the man who lives unafraid of blame, a mere cow, grieves the heart by eating rice
the man who abandoned the hard penance he had taken up grieves the heart by eating rice
the married man who lives in fear of his wife, an ox, grieves the heart by eating rice

norm.note: a period judgment on a husband who lives in fear of his wife

80.reading: Leadership gained by one who does not rule justly, penance taken up by one without restraint of heart, and beauty gained by one who does not make his conduct perfect are named seed scattered into a thicket.
80.nuance: Each item is a gain (rank, penance, beauty) that comes to someone who lacks its inner condition, so the waste lies in the receiver, not in the gift.

items.claim: headship won by one who does not do justice is seed thrown into a thicket
penance taken up by one without inner restraint is seed thrown into a thicket
beauty in one who does not perfect his conduct is seed thrown into a thicket

links.note: The Kural gives guarding against what is coming as a mark of understanding; the verse makes it one of a great minister's three daily practices.
links.teaches: Foresight that the Kural praises as a private wisdom becomes, in a minister, an office: one prevents the blow by knowing the enemy king's state every day.
links.list_adds: It binds foresight to self-discipline and daily watch on hostile kings, so prevention is shown as the minister's working method rather than a trait.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu 30 names as sweet the three virtues whose breach Thirikadugam 62 counts: weighing a kindness, no crooked word in the assembly, not seizing a deposit.
links.teaches: The two books count the same three acts of trust from both sides, sweetness for keeping them and loss of heirs for breaking them, so the triad was a fixed set in the period's teaching.

links.note: The Kural says the upright man's wealth is a strength to his descendants; Thirikadugam says the man who speaks crookedly in the assembly loses his descendants.
links.teaches: Read together, fairness and its breach are both paid in the next generation: the Kural's promise to the heirs of the just has its dark twin in the heirless partial judge.
links.list_adds: It sets partial speech beside ingratitude and a seized deposit, so unfairness is classed as a breach of trust with a shared penalty.

links.note: Verse 64 makes tending guests the duty by which a chaste wife is a friend; verse 63 counts a bangled wife who dreads guests among things that yield no good.
links.teaches: The two adjacent verses give the same rule from both sides: hospitality is the wife's first duty, and failing it alone makes her a loss to the house.

links.note: The Kural calls good children the ornament of a house's excellence; the verse makes bearing children of an old family the act by which the wife is mistress of the house.
links.teaches: Children move from ornament to office: what the Kural treats as the crown of a good home, Thirikadugam treats as a debt the wife owes in order to hold her title.
links.list_adds: It turns three household goods into three roles of one woman, friend, mother and mistress, and frames them all as debts of chastity.

links.note: The Kural names desire, anger and confusion as the triad whose very names must perish; the verse counts fear, craving and anger as self-consuming.
links.teaches: Fear takes the place of confusion: Thirikadugam treats terror as a passion of the same kind as craving and anger, burning the one who holds it, which the Kural's triad leaves out.
links.list_adds: It replaces confusion with fear and gives the triad an image of self-frying in one's own ghee, so the harm is shown as self-inflicted.

links.note: The Kural says the king who bends the sceptre loses wealth and people together; the verse counts the bent-sceptred king among things not joined with fitness.
links.teaches: Besides the ruin the Kural predicts, the unjust king is also absurd, like a ring on a man with no servant: injustice is shown as a failure of seemliness as well as of rule.
links.list_adds: It sets the unjust king beside a husbandless woman's ornament and a servantless man's ring, so royal injustice is judged as an empty sign of rank.

links.note: Naladiyar 363 calls three kinds of wife weapons that kill the husband; Thirikadugam 67 counts the wife who stands against her husband with bad servants and faulty kin as old karma that devours him.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar blames the wife as an agent, while Thirikadugam spreads the harm across the whole household and calls it past karma with no remedy, shifting from blame to endurance.
links.list_adds: It widens the Naladiyar's three bad wives to wife, servants and kin, and explains them as karma ripening in old age.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 61 counts kin, wife, servant, son and neighbour as five household diseases; Thirikadugam 67 counts wife, servants and kin as devouring old karma.
links.teaches: Two counted works single out the same household cast as a chronic affliction; Sirupanchamoolam calls it disease and adds son and neighbour, Thirikadugam calls it karma and adds old age.

links.note: The Kural calls not hurting others the settled stand of the stainless; the verse names doing no hurt to any creature as purity itself.
links.teaches: The Kural's stainless people are defined by harmlessness, and Thirikadugam draws the conclusion that harmlessness simply is purity, setting it against ritual senses of the word.
links.list_adds: It sets purity as harmlessness beside giving to the poor and a life shaped by impermanence, as the three marks of those who know the good.

links.note: The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; the verse lists giving to the needy and the path of one who considers impermanence side by side.
links.teaches: The Kural derives giving from impermanence as a single argument; Thirikadugam presents them as two coordinate marks of the wise, so awareness of transience is a conduct in its own right.
links.list_adds: It lists giving and awareness of impermanence as separate items with harmlessness, rather than deriving one from the other.

links.note: The Kural measures the fruit of hospitality by the guest's worth; the verse prizes the guest who comes in distress after losing his way.
links.teaches: Against the Kural's ranking of guests by merit, Thirikadugam values the guest by his need: the lost and suffering stranger is the rare prize.
links.list_adds: It counts the lost guest among hard-to-get goods with a working ox and a maiden, so the guest is valued as a gain to the house, not a cost.

links.note: Verse 69 counts the lost, suffering guest as hard to come by; verse 76 counts the guest who arrives on a rainy day as hard to tend.
links.teaches: The same book holds both sides of hospitality: the needy guest is a rare prize and also the hardest burden, so the value and the strain of the guest come together.

links.note: The Kural likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank filling; the verse calls the man who dug a charitable tank and grove one of the truly rich.
links.teaches: The Kural's simile is made literal: the public tank is not only like a good man's wealth, its digging is counted as his wealth.
links.list_adds: It redefines the rich as three givers, of a tank, of Vedic learning and of shared food, so wealth is measured by what one has made common.

links.note: The Kural likens the brief want of the renowned rich to rain-clouds running dry; the verse counts the poverty of men with the manliness to give as a sight the eye cannot bear.
links.teaches: Both treat a giver's poverty as a public loss rather than a private one; Thirikadugam adds the witness's pain, so the giver's want hurts those who watch.
links.list_adds: It sets the giver's poverty beside two shameful sights, so the generous man's want is ranked as a kind of indignity.

links.note: The Kural tells one to let go that day of gain that comes from leaving fairness; the verse says ill-gotten wealth itself fears the man who keeps dharma in mind.
links.teaches: The Kural asks for an act of renunciation, while Thirikadugam makes it a property of the person: for the dharma-minded, wrong gain never comes near enough to refuse.
links.list_adds: It sets dharma beside steadiness and valour as three strengths that make things fear their holder, a ranking of inner strengths the couplet lacks.

links.note: The Kural calls nothing harder than the hardness that would end poverty by begging; the verse counts the man who would build wealth by begging among three who dare the hard.
links.teaches: Thirikadugam pushes the Kural's case further: begging not to escape poverty but to grow rich, and it ranks this with crossing the sea as a reckless venture.
links.list_adds: It sets begging-for-wealth beside trusting a roving woman and a sea voyage, so the folly is judged as a physical gamble.

links.note: The Kural says the asker's heart rejoices at givers who give without scorn; the verse counts the man who laughs at one asking for a gift among those who hold to nothing.
links.teaches: The Kural shows the asker's side and Thirikadugam the scorner's: mocking an asker is not just meanness but a sign of a man without any principle.
links.list_adds: It sets mocking a beggar beside killing to eat and presuming on the great, so contempt for the asker is ranked with flesh-eating as a lack of rule.

links.note: The Kural says killing is the absence of grace and eating the flesh is not right; the verse counts the man who lives by killing and eating among three who keep no rule.
links.teaches: The Kural argues from grace, Thirikadugam from discipline: flesh-eating is condemned on both grounds, in one as cruelty and in the other as want of a firm rule.
links.list_adds: It sets killing to eat among faults of social conduct, so non-killing is read as part of self-rule rather than of compassion alone.

links.note: Naladiyar 386 uses the learning of a man with understanding and bright wealth in a generous man's hands as similes for a modest woman's beauty; Thirikadugam 75 counts the same two as solid heartwood.
links.teaches: The same paired figures served two works with different ends: the Naladiyar borrows them to praise a woman's beauty, Thirikadugam keeps them as goods in their own right with a heartwood image.
links.list_adds: It treats the two figures as things in themselves, joined by a leader who knows fit unions, under one tree image.

links.note: The Kural likens wealth in a just man's hands to a fruit tree ripening in town; the verse likens wealth in a generous man's hands to a tree hardened without hollow.
links.teaches: Both use a tree for the good man's wealth, but the Kural praises its fruit given to all and Thirikadugam the soundness of its wood, so the same image teaches use and durability.
links.list_adds: It sets wealth beside learning and a fit leader as three sound trees, ranking generosity with understanding.

links.note: The Kural says men of unsteady heart touch women who join with them while their hearts are elsewhere; the verse counts the courtesan whose heart is elsewhere yet never fails in business as hard to keep.
links.teaches: Both note the courtesan's divided heart; Thirikadugam adds that her business never fails, so the danger is a reliable trade without love.
links.list_adds: It sets the courtesan beside a rain-day guest and a defiant servant, so she is counted among household burdens rather than vices.

links.note: The Kural says those who resolve to live by a spotless lineage do nothing unworthy through deceit; the verse says three positive habits are found only in those of spotless family.
links.teaches: The Kural shows lineage as a restraint on wrongdoing; Thirikadugam shows it as a source of positive conduct, so a pure line both forbids and produces.
links.list_adds: It names three habits of a good family, avoiding the base, constancy in friendship and guarding against blame, where the couplet gives one restraint.

links.note: The Kural says inner purity is seen through truth; the verse counts purity, truth and evil unspoken in mind and word as the ascetic's practice.
links.teaches: The Kural ties purity to truth; Thirikadugam gives each its own fruit, boldness and beauty, and adds silence of the mind as a third discipline.
links.list_adds: It separates purity and truth into two items with different rewards and places them in the ascetic's domain.

links.note: Verse 78 names the practices of those strong in penance; verse 80 counts penance taken up by one without restraint of heart as wasted seed.
links.teaches: The two verses together give the condition and its failure: penance bears fruit with purity and restraint of mind, and is seed lost in a thicket without them.

links.note: The Kural says penance comes to those who have it and is futile for others; the verse counts penance taken up by one without restraint as seed cast in a thicket.
links.teaches: Thirikadugam names what the Kural leaves circular: the missing quality is restraint of the heart, so the futility is located in the will.
links.list_adds: It ranks futile penance with unjust headship and unruly beauty, so the failure is shown as a general rule of gifts without their inner condition.

links.note: The Kural says beauty without subtle understanding is a clay doll; the verse says beauty in one who does not perfect his conduct is wasted seed.
links.teaches: The two place the condition of beauty in different places, learning for the Kural and conduct for Thirikadugam, so beauty needs both mind and conduct to count.
links.list_adds: It moves the test of beauty from understanding to conduct and sets it with rank and penance.

links.note: The Kural says the man who fears his wife fears to do good to the good; the verse calls the man who lives in fear of his wife an ox whose eating grieves the heart.
links.teaches: The Kural names the harm, Thirikadugam the scorn: a wife-fearing husband is useless to others and also a beast, set beside the shameless and the lapsed ascetic.
links.list_adds: It ranks the wife-fearing husband with the blame-fearless man and the lapsed ascetic, as three who should not even be fed.

source_issues: thirikadugam 76 line 1: the text reads வருந்தும் where the sense and tamilvu have விருந்தும் (guest); the item is copied as written.
